description:
KerBeroS is a team passionate about technology, science, innovation, and space exploration. We believe that great ideas can become meaningful solutions when creativity, collaboration, and technology come together.

Our background includes software development, backend engineering, Java, Spring Boot, cloud technologies, and building scalable solutions. We are excited to apply our technical knowledge and problem-solving mindset to real-world challenges using NASA's open data and resources.
summary:
AGRO-SCOPE is a web dashboard that helps farmers and agronomists explore how different crop rotations would use water in their field before they plant. Our pilot is the Virú Valley in La Libertad, Peru, an irrigated desert valley where water is the main constraint for small and medium farms.

The tool combines NASA POWER daily climate data (2001–2025) with transparent, reproducible FAO-56 models: reference evapotranspiration (Penman–Monteith), crop water demand, and a root-zone soil water balance. It compares three illustrative strategies (continuous corn, corn–bean–corn, and corn–potato–corn) and reports crop water demand, modeled actual evapotranspiration, water deficit, deep percolation, and water-stress days. Users can edit scenarios, view the pilot area on an interactive map, and switch between English and Spanish.

This addresses Field Shift by turning NASA Earth observations into rotation comparisons that a farmer can question and discuss. Every number shows its source and its limits: observations, model outputs, and synthetic test inputs are clearly separated, and the tool supports rather than replaces local expertise. It matters because rotation choices made without water information can deplete scarce irrigation supplies and soils.
details:
What it does

AGRO-SCOPE is a web dashboard for exploring how crop-rotation strategies would use water in an irrigated valley before anyone plants. Our pilot is the Virú Valley (La Libertad, Peru), a coastal desert valley where irrigation water is the main constraint for small and medium farms. The dashboard has four parts:

  • Pilot area: an interactive map of the study polygon, clearly labeled as provisional (not an official or cadastral boundary).
  • Climate data: NASA POWER daily data for seven parameters (temperature, humidity, wind, solar radiation and precipitation) from 2001 to 2025, with time series, monthly summaries, units, provenance and missing-data status.
  • Science chain: reference evapotranspiration (FAO-56 Penman–Monteith), crop water demand (FAO-56 single crop coefficient) and a root-zone soil water balance.
  • Rotation comparison: three illustrative strategies (continuous corn, corn → bean → corn, corn → potato → corn), reporting crop water demand, modeled actual evapotranspiration, water deficit, deep percolation and water-stress days. Users can edit scenarios and enter field context in the browser.

How it works

Python modules download NASA POWER data, run quality checks, and compute ET₀, ETc and the soil water balance. The outputs are saved as traceable CSV and JSON files with metadata, and the React app reads them at build time. A 30-day synthetic scenario tests the full ET₀ → ETc → water-balance chain, and unit tests cover each scientific module.

Benefits and intended impact

  • Turns NASA Earth observations into numbers a farmer or extension agronomist can question: how much water each rotation would need, and when the crop would run short.
  • Supports conversations about adding legumes or other crops to break continuous corn, using the same transparent method for every option.
  • Is designed to grow into a decision-support tool for other irrigated valleys: the pilot geometry, crop and soil catalogs and scenarios are all configuration files.

What makes it creative

Instead of a black-box recommendation, every value carries its label: observation, model output or synthetic test input. The interface states what each result does and does not mean, so the tool supports local expertise rather than replacing it. The full dashboard is available in English and Spanish, so it serves both international reviewers and Peruvian farmers.

Factors our team considered

  • Scale: NASA POWER is a point estimate near the pilot centroid, not a polygon average.
  • Honesty about data: satellite catalogs (GPM IMERG, MODIS NDVI and ET, Landsat) were queried, but their rasters are not shown as processed observations until they actually are.
  • Provisional parameters: crop and soil parameters are generic FAO values pending local validation.
  • Fair comparison: strategies have different durations, so cumulative totals are interpreted with care.
  • No overreach: the tool makes no yield predictions, irrigation prescriptions or automatic crop recommendations.

Tools and technologies

  • Frontend: React 18, TypeScript, Vite, Leaflet / React-Leaflet, Lucide icons.
  • Science: Python 3.10+ (acquisition, quality control, FAO-56 models, automated tests).
  • Data: NASA POWER API, NASA CMR / STAC catalog queries, GeoJSON (WGS 84).
  • Delivery: GitHub, Docker, nginx, Google Cloud Build and Cloud Run.

GPM IMERG precipitation (catalog query; not yet processed)
MODIS MOD13Q1 v061 Vegetation Indices / NDVI (catalog query; not yet processed)
MODIS MOD16A2 v061 Evapotranspiration (catalog query; not yet processed)
ECOSTRESS ECO_L2T_LSTE v002 Land Surface Temperature (catalog query; not yet processed)
ECOSTRESS ECO_L3T_JET v002 Evapotranspiration (catalog query; not yet processed)
SMAP SPL3SMP_E v6 Enhanced Soil Moisture (catalog query; not yet processed)
Landsat Collection 2 Level-2 (NASA/USGS; STAC catalog query)
